questions.stem: Stars begin their lives as…

options.text: a nebula — a giant cloud of gas and dust
options.explanation: The nebula is stage one for every star.
White dwarfs are the end of the road, not the start.
Red giants come after the main sequence.
Supernovae end the largest stars' lives.

questions.stem: What force pulls a nebula into a protostar?

options.explanation: Fusion starts only after the protostar is hot enough.

options.text: gravity, pulling the particles closer together
options.explanation: Gravity drives the collapse.
Gravity, not magnetism, does the gathering.
Light pressure is not the collapsing agent.

questions.stem: As the protostar's density increases, its temperature…

options.explanation: The temperature climbs during collapse.
Nothing cools to zero here.

options.text: increases, because collisions between particles become more frequent
options.explanation: More crowding means more collisions and more heating.

options.text: decreases, because the particles spread out
options.explanation: Collapsing crowds particles, it does not spread them.

questions.stem: A protostar becomes a main sequence star when…

options.explanation: Running out comes billions of years later.

options.text: it collapses into a white dwarf
options.explanation: That is the solar-mass ending.
Only the most massive stars do that.

options.text: it becomes hot enough for nuclear fusion to begin in its core
options.explanation: Fusion ignition is the promotion criterion.

questions.stem: Which sequence opens a star's life story, starting from a nebula?

options.explanation: All stars follow the same opening stages.
The nebula comes first.
The red giant is a late stage.
The main sequence follows ignition.

questions.stem: State what a nebula is.
questions.modelAnswer: A nebula is an enormous drifting cloud of gas and dust, and stars form inside it.

questions.stem: Describe how a protostar forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Gravity draws the nebula's particles inward until a hot ball of gas forms — the protostar.

questions.stem: Explain why a collapsing protostar gets hotter.
questions.modelAnswer: As gravity packs the particles closer, the density rises and collisions between particles become more frequent, and those more frequent collisions raise the temperature.

questions.stem: A cloud of gas is collapsing. State the stage it has reached once it is a hot, dense ball but fusion has not yet started.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a protostar: fusion ignition, which would promote it to a main sequence star, has not yet begun.

questions.stem: A main sequence star is stable because…

options.explanation: Collapse ended at the protostar stage.

options.text: it is in equilibrium during its fusion-powered life
options.explanation: Equilibrium is the main-sequence state.
Fusion is what powers the main sequence.
Expansion belongs to the red giant stage.

questions.stem: What triggers the red giant stage?

options.explanation: Solar-mass stars never explode.
Helium fusion is what happens next, not what stops.

options.text: the hydrogen in the core beginning to run out
options.explanation: Fuel exhaustion starts the transition.

options.text: the star colliding with a nebula
options.explanation: Collisions are not part of the sequence.

questions.stem: During the red giant stage the star…

options.explanation: That describes the white dwarf turn.
The star swells dramatically.
Hydrogen is fading, not accelerating.

options.text: expands outward as its surface cools
options.explanation: Helium fusion swells the outer layers; expansion cools them.

questions.stem: After the main sequence, a Sun-like star becomes…

options.explanation: Red giant precedes the white dwarf for solar-mass stars.
Only much larger stars go supernova.
That follows supernovae of big stars.
Stages do not rewind.

questions.stem: The star begins to fuse which fuel as it turns into a red giant?

options.explanation: Uranium is a fission fuel, not a stellar fuel.
Helium fusion swells the outer layers.
Carbon comes later, in larger stars.
Iron belongs to the most massive stars.

questions.stem: State the stage a star enters once fusion starts in its core.
questions.modelAnswer: It becomes a main sequence star and is in stable equilibrium.

questions.stem: Name the stage after the main sequence for a Sun-like star.
questions.modelAnswer: The star becomes a red giant.

questions.stem: Explain why the star expands when the red giant stage begins.
questions.modelAnswer: With the hydrogen fading, the star starts fusing helium, and those reactions push the outer layers outward — the star swells while its surface cools.

questions.stem: A star has burned most of its core hydrogen. State the next two stages it passes through.
questions.modelAnswer: It next becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf.

questions.stem: What does a solar-mass star become when helium fusion ends?

options.explanation: Solar-mass stars shed no supernova.
Black holes need far more mass.

options.text: a white dwarf, as the star collapses
options.explanation: Collapse after helium exhaustion forms the white dwarf.
Stages do not repeat backwards.

questions.stem: Over time a white dwarf…

options.explanation: It cools, it does not climb.
The fuel is gone.
No re-expansion happens.

options.text: cools down and emits decreasing energy
options.explanation: Cooling is the white dwarf's whole career.

questions.stem: A black dwarf is…

options.text: a white dwarf that has cooled until it no longer emits light
options.explanation: The fully faded endpoint carries the 'black' name.
It is the cooled endpoint of a formed star.

options.text: a nebula ready to form stars
options.explanation: Nebulae are birthplaces, not endings.

options.text: another name for a black hole
options.explanation: Black holes form from the most massive stars.

questions.stem: What does a solar-mass star collapse into once helium fusion finishes?

options.explanation: That is the large-star path.

options.text: a white dwarf, once helium fusion finishes
options.explanation: Collapse follows the end of helium fusion.

options.text: main sequence → white dwarf → red giant
options.explanation: The dwarf comes last.

options.text: red giant → main sequence → white dwarf
options.explanation: The main sequence comes first.

questions.stem: As the white dwarf cools, the energy it emits…

options.explanation: The emission declines as it cools.
Nothing restarts high-energy emission.
Cooling output falls in step with temperature.
Cooling means less emission.

questions.stem: State what a star becomes when its helium fusion finishes.
questions.modelAnswer: Collapse sets in, and the star becomes a white dwarf.

questions.stem: State what a white dwarf eventually becomes.
questions.modelAnswer: It cools until it no longer emits light and becomes a black dwarf.

questions.stem: Explain why a white dwarf's light output falls over time.
questions.modelAnswer: The white dwarf has no fusion left to feed it, so it simply cools; as its temperature drops, the energy it emits decreases until it no longer emits light.

questions.stem: Order the full solar-mass biography: white dwarf, nebula, red giant, main sequence star.
questions.modelAnswer: Nebula → main sequence star → red giant → white dwarf.
